title: Simplified Writing: Back to the Future
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Underwood responds, partly with sarcasm, to a Reading League book-club presentation on The Writing Revolution that treats writing as a linear, separable set of stages starting with outlining. He contrasts this with the composition-theory tradition he was trained in, in which writing processes are recursive, vary by purpose and context, and use drafting as a way to discover ideas. He questions the claims that planning should be taught to mastery before drafting and that skills such as decoding must precede writing. His own classroom experience, in which reluctant readers engaged through the agency they found in writing, is offered as counter-evidence. The piece is an opinionated defense of process-based writing instruction against Science of Reading influence on writing pedagogy.
points: The presentation recasts writing as discrete, separately teachable stages beginning with outlining, rejecting the recursive view of composition.
Underwood cites evidence that students often write the paper first and then produce the required outline.
He argues revision is where writers talk through problems and follow ideas, not something prewriting exists to make less painful.
The argument that drafting overloads working memory is used to defer drafting, which he sees as undermining discovery and audience awareness.
He notes the political reach of the Science of Reading movement into state legislation as a reason for concern over writing standards.
quotes: So what I learned about the history of composition theory in my doctoral program was all wrong. My professors fooled me into thinking writing instruction is more complex than it really is. My experience in the Area III Writing Project was illegitimate.

It was gut wrenching, not because I hadn’t heard this view before, but because this Science of Reading movement has made such inroads into state legislation. I heard that my colleagues and I have been wrong all these years.

Writing teachers should have been teaching children to plan first in linear fashion, and planning involves outlining, which controls what can be written in a draft. I remember a study showing that when teachers required students to submit an outline with a paper, many of them wrote the paper first and then prepared an outline.

If you read the right hand sidebar in the screenshot above, you’ll learn that planning makes revision less “painful.” I taught my kids that revision was the most exciting part—writers could talk with others about writing problems and opportunities, follow up on ideas that surfaced during drafting, draft some more as they understood more about why they were writing the piece in the first place.

How could we have expected children to draft without knowing what they would like to say in advance? How could we have worked so hard to help writers develop a sense of audience when they can’t yet plan a linear outline? Why would we invite them to bypass orthographic mapping and invent spellings just to write a poem?
I found just the reverse when I taught fourth grade. My reluctant readers turned on to reading gradually as they learned about agency through writing. But agency has no place in writing instruction.
